title: "Multi-Source ETL Pipeline for Supplier Spend Analysis"
description: "Built a Snowflake data pipeline pulling purchase orders, supplier invoices, and geospatial data from three different source formats to answer one question: are we being invoiced what we were quoted?"
date: 2025-06-15

## The Business Question

Every purchase order carries an expected price. Every supplier invoice carries what actually got billed. When those two numbers drift apart across thousands of orders, nobody notices row by row; it shows up as margin leakage a quarter later. This project (a team assignment; my role was building and owning the pipeline) set out to make that drift visible at the transaction level, automatically, instead of after the fact.

## The Data Problem

The inputs didn't live in one place or one format: monthly purchase-order extracts as CSVs, supplier invoice records in a Postgres database, supplier contact/location data in XML, and a public U.S. Census ZCTA gazetteer file for geocoding supplier locations. Before any analysis could happen, all four had to land in the same warehouse in a shape that could actually be joined.

## Data Model

I mapped the underlying Procure-to-Pay structure, suppliers, purchase orders, receiving reports, and supplier invoices, before writing a single COPY statement, since a bad join here silently corrupts the variance calculation downstream:

![Procure-to-Pay entity relationship diagram: suppliers, purchase orders, receiving reports, and invoices](../../images/projects/sql/erd-procure-to-pay.png){fig-alt="Entity relationship diagram showing Supplier, SupplierLocation, PurchaseOrderHeader, PurchaseOrderLine, ReceivingReportHeader, ReceivingReportLine, and SupplierInvoice tables with their keys and relationships"}

## Pipeline

I built a Python-orchestrated pipeline (`pipeline_runner.py`) that exports the Postgres invoice table to CSV, stages all three source formats into Snowflake internal stages, `COPY INTO`s them into raw tables with tolerant staging (numeric and date fields loaded as text first, then normalized, since messy real-world CSVs break strict-typed loads), normalizes order dates into a consistent format, and geocodes supplier ZIP codes against the ZCTA gazetteer using `TO_GEOGRAPHY` for spatial joins.

On top of the raw tables, I layered views that total purchase-order amounts, aggregate invoice line items per order, and finally join the two:

```sql
create or replace table purchase_orders_and_invoices as
with inv_ex as (
  select purchaseorderid, sum(amount_ex_tax) as amount_ex_tax
  from v_supplier_invoices group by purchaseorderid
)
select p.purchaseorderid, p.supplierid, p.orderdate_norm,
       p.POAmount, inv_ex.amount_ex_tax,
       (inv_ex.amount_ex_tax - p.POAmount) as invoiced_vs_quoted
from v_po_amounts p
join inv_ex on inv_ex.purchaseorderid = p.purchaseorderid;
```

`invoiced_vs_quoted` is the column the whole pipeline exists to produce: a per-order variance that can be sorted, thresholded, and handed to a procurement team as an exception list instead of a full re-audit.

## Why It Matters

This is the unglamorous half of analytics that most portfolios skip: before you can build a dashboard or a model, the data has to actually be trustworthy and joinable. Tolerant staging, explicit normalization steps, and verification queries against `COPY_HISTORY` were as important to getting a correct answer here as the final variance formula, and this is exactly the kind of pipeline work a business or data analyst role expects you to be comfortable owning yourself, not just consuming secondhand.
